sceneHappening: No favoritism toward the rich; the royal law of love; faith without works is dead
summary: "My brothers, don't hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of glory with partiality. For if a man with a gold ring, in fine clothing, comes into your synagogue, and a poor man in filthy clothing also comes in, and you pay special attention to him who wears the fine clothing and say, 'Sit here in a good place;' and you tell the poor man, 'Stand there,' or 'Sit by my footstool' haven't you shown partiality among yourselves, and become judges with evil thoughts?" "Didn't God choose those who are poor in this world to be rich in faith, and heirs of the Kingdom which he promised to those who love him? But you have dishonored the poor man. Don't the rich oppress you, and personally drag you before the courts? Don't they blaspheme the honorable name by which you are called?" "If you fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself,' you do well. But if you show partiality, you commit sin." "Whoever keeps the whole law, and yet stumbles in one point, he has become guilty of all." "So speak and so do, as men who are to be judged by a law of freedom. For judgment is without mercy to him who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment." Then the question of faith: "What good is it, my brothers, if a man says he has faith, but has no works? Can faith save him? And if a brother or sister is naked and in lack of daily food, and one of you tells them, 'Go in peace. Be warmed and filled;' yet you didn't give them the things the body needs, what good is it? Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself." "You believe that God is one. You do well. The demons also believe, and shudder." "Wasn't Abraham our father justified by works, in that he offered up Isaac his son on the altar? You see that faith worked with his works, and by works faith was perfected. So the Scripture was fulfilled which says, 'Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him as righteousness,' and he was called the friend of God. You see then that by works, a man is justified, and not only by faith. In the same way, wasn't Rahab the prostitute also justified by works, in that she received the messengers and sent them out another way? For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, even so faith apart from works is dead."
whySettingMatters: The scene in 2:2-4 is of a gathering (literally "synagogue," the word for an assembly, used here for a Christian meeting) in which a rich man is given the best seat and a poor man is told to stand or sit on the floor. The "royal law" (2:8) is the command to love one's neighbor (Leviticus 19:18), which Jesus called the second great commandment (Matthew 22:39); calling it "royal" may mean it is the king's own law or that it rules over the rest. The verse that whoever breaks one point is "guilty of all" (2:10) says the law is a single whole, not that every sin is equally serious. The passage on faith and works (2:14-26) is the best-known and most debated in the letter, because it can sound like a contradiction of Paul (Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16). Most readers have noted that the two use the words differently: Paul argues that a person is put right with God by trusting Christ and not by keeping the law as a way to earn it; James argues that a faith that produces nothing is not real faith. "Justified" in James may mean "declared righteous" or "shown to be righteous"; "works" in James are acts of mercy and obedience, not the ritual works of the law Paul argues against; and both use Abraham and Genesis 15:6 to different ends. Some think James is answering a distorted version of Paul's teaching. The example of the demons (2:19) shows that agreeing that "God is one" (the Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4) can be only a statement; Rahab (Joshua 2) is a surprising second example, a foreign woman who acted on what she believed. "Friend of God" for Abraham comes from Isaiah 41:8 and 2 Chronicles 20:7.

people.note: Warns against partiality and presses the link between faith and works.
Told not to favor the rich or dishonor the poor.
Seen oppressing believers and dragging them to court.
Chosen by God to be rich in faith.
Called "our Lord Jesus Christ of glory."

questions: James says favoritism turns people into "judges with evil thoughts." What judgments are made about people in our own gatherings?
"Mercy triumphs over judgment." How does this change the way you hold the law?
What does "faith without works is dead" mean to you, and how would you reconcile it with Paul's "by faith, not works"?
The demons believe and shudder. What is the difference between that kind of believing and the kind James wants?

"Into your synagogue" (2:2). The word means an assembly.
"A gold ring" (2:2). The word appears only here.
"In fine clothing" (2:2-3). The word means shining.
"In filthy clothing" (2:2). The word appears only here.
"Haven't you shown partiality" (2:4). The Greek is "haven't you made distinctions."
"Didn't God choose those who are poor" (2:5).
"To be rich in faith" (2:5) and "don't the rich oppress you" (2:6).
"Which he promised to those who love him" (2:5).
"But you have dishonored the poor man" (2:6).
"The name by which you are called" (2:7).
"You shall love your neighbor as yourself" (2:8).
"Without mercy" (2:13). The word appears only here.
"Triumphs over judgment" (2:13). The word means to boast over.
"But has no works" (2:14), "by my works" (2:18), and "by works" (2:21-25).

"It was accounted to him as righteousness" (2:23).
